παρδαλεων. περι δε των κυνων τι δει και λεγειν; ως τους νεους τε και λιπαρους αυτων εσθιουσι παμπολλοι, οντα τα τοιαυτα παντα ξηροτατα φυσει και δριμειαν τροφην παρεχοντα τῳ σωματι και παρα τους τροπους δε των σκευασιων αυτων μαλλον η ηττον τρεφει, και μαλλον και ηττον πεττεται. οσα μεν γαρ οπτωντες η τηγανιζοντες εσθιουσι, ξηροτεραν τροφην διδωσι τῳ σωματι· οσα δε εψοντες και αρτυοντες προσφερονται μεταξυ τουτων εισι. και αυτων δε τουτων ου μικρα διαφορα γιγνεται παρα τον της αρτυσεως τροπον. και δια ταυτα ξηραινειν μεν θελων το σωμα των ξηροτερων τῃ κρασει ζῳων δωσεις την σαρκα, θερμαινειν δε βουλομενος των θερμοτερων και ψυχροτερων και υγροτερων ομοιως τοις καταλληλοις δωσεις.
translation: About meat, from Galen. Not all meat of animals nourishes humans, but that of some is even deadly, while others are administered not only as nourishment, but also as a remedy. And not all of those that nourish have the same capacity. Now, of all kinds of meat that of pigs is the most nutritious, and it produces good humours and is the easiest to digest of all, among other things also because of its similarity with man. Beef gives nourishment that is neither inconsiderable nor easily dispersed, yet it generates thicker blood than is suitable, and if someone is of a rather ‘melancholic’ mixture, he will be seized by one of the melancholic affections if he eats it to excess. Affections of this kind are: cancer, elephas, leichēn, mange, quartan fever and what is properly called melancholia. And in some people the spleen is affected because of this humour, upon which a bad state of dropsy often follows. For cattle are altogether drier and hotter than pigs. Young bulls have meat that is better for digestion than that of full-grown cattle, being of a wetter mixture. Likewise kids are also better than goats. For goats are less dry in their mixture than cattle, but compared to humans or pigs they differ greatly. Lambs have meat that is very wet and apt to produce phlegm, and the meat of sheep is rather full of residues and produces bad humours. The meat of goats, too, produces bad humours [combined] with sharpness. That of the he-goat is the worst when it comes to both good humours and coction, followed by that of rams and then that of bulls. In all of these [animals], the meat of castrated ones is better. Older animals are worst when it comes to coction, good humours and nourishment, so that even among the very pigs, although they are wet in their mixture, the aged ones have fibrous, hard and dry - and therefore hard to digest - meat. And the meat of the hare generates rather thick blood, but it is better for good humours than beef or lamb. The meat of deer is no less apt to produce bad humours, and it is also hard, and difficult to digest. That of wild donkeys - for some eat even that, just as they eat that of domesticated donkeys in Alexandria - is strongly apt to produce bad humours and hard to digest and bad for the stomach, and furthermore unpleasant to eat, as is that of horses and camels. For people who are ass-like and camel-like in their souls and bodies eat that, too. Some even take the meat of bears and the even worse meats of lions and panthers. And what should I even say about dog meat? Because a great many people eat young and fat ones. These are all very dry by nature and provide sharp nourishment for the body, and according to the ways of preparing them they nourish more or less and are digested more or less well. For the meat that they eat baked or pan-fried provides a drier nourishment for the body, while meat that they take boiled and seasoned is halfway between these. And among these, a considerable difference arises according to the way it is seasoned. And because of that, if you want to dry the body, you will give the meat of animals that are drier in their mixtures, while if you want to heat it, of the hotter ones, and of the colder and wetter ones you will also likewise give to the corresponding ones.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῶν ἐν τοῖς πεζοῖς ζῴοις ἄκρων
greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν αὐτάρκη σοι καθόλου περὶ τῆς τῶν πεζῶν ζῴων σαρκὸς ἀκηκοέναι· περὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων μορίων ὧν ἔχει τὰ ζῷα τῆς δυνάμεως ἐφεξῆς ἄκουε. ἄκρεα μόρια καλοῦσι συνήθως ἄνθρωποι πόδας καὶ ῥύγχη καὶ ὦτα· ἥκιστα μὲν γὰρ πιμελὴν ἔχει ταῦτα, ἥκιστα δὲ τὴν σαρκώδη φύσιν· ἐπικρατεῖ δὲ ἐν αὐτοῖς τὸ τε νευρῶδες καὶ τὸ δερματῶδες. γεγύμνασται δὲ τῇ πολλῇ κινήσει ταῦτα τὰ μέρη μᾶλλον· ἐστὶ δὲ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ γλισχρότερα. εἰκότως οὖν ἐλάττονα μὲν τροφὴν δίδωσι τῷ σώματι, ῥᾷον δὲ ὑπέρχεται κατὰ γαστέρα διὰ τὴν γλισχρότητα, βελτίους δὲ οἱ πόδες τῶν ὑῶν εἰσι τοῦ ῥύγχους, ὥσπερ καὶ τοῦτο τῶν ὤτων.
greek_normalized: ταυτα μεν ουν αυταρκη σοι καθολου περι της των πεζων ζῳων σαρκος ακηκοεναι· περι δε των αλλων μοριων ων εχει τα ζῳα της δυναμεως εφεξης ακουε. ακρεα μορια καλουσι συνηθως ανθρωποι ποδας και ρυγχη και ωτα· ηκιστα μεν γαρ πιμελην εχει ταυτα, ηκιστα δε την σαρκωδη φυσιν· επικρατει δε εν αυτοις το τε νευρωδες και το δερματωδες. γεγυμνασται δε τῃ πολλῃ κινησει ταυτα τα μερη μαλλον· εστι δε δια τουτο και γλισχροτερα. εικοτως ουν ελαττονα μεν τροφην διδωσι τῳ σωματι, ρᾳον δε υπερχεται κατα γαστερα δια την γλισχροτητα, βελτιους δε οι ποδες των υων εισι του ρυγχους, ωσπερ και τουτο των ωτων.
translation: About the extremities of land animals. Now, this was sufficient for you to hear about the meat of land animals altogether, but hear in the following about the other parts in which animals have a capacity. People habitually call the feet and the snout and the ears the fleshless parts. For these have the least fat and the least amount of a fleshy nature, and the nerve-like and skin-like prevails in them. These parts are more exercised by much movement, and because of that they are also rather slippery. Accordingly, then, they give less nourishment to the body, and they pass more easily in the stomach because of their slipperiness. The feet of pigs are better than the snout, just as the latter is better than the ears.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῆς ἐν τοῖς πεζοῖς ζῴοις γλώττης
greek: χαυνοτέρα δὲ καὶ ἀναιμοτέρα τῆς γλώττης ἡ ἰδία σάρξ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ψαφαρωτέρα καὶ πέττεσθαι ῥᾳδίως δυναμένη χωρὶς ἐπιμιξίας τῶν περικειμένων αὐτῇ ἑτέρων.
greek_normalized: χαυνοτερα δε και αναιμοτερα της γλωττης η ιδια σαρξ, και δια τουτο και ψαφαρωτερα και πεττεσθαι ρᾳδιως δυναμενη χωρις επιμιξιας των περικειμενων αυτῃ ετερων.
translation: About the tongue of land animals. The meat proper to tongues is looser and more bloodless, and because of that it is of a rather loose texture and it can easily be digested without being combined with other parts that surround it.

greek: πάντων ἀδένων κοινόν, ἡδεῖς τε καὶ ψαθυροὺς φαίνεσθαι κατὰ τὴν ἐδωδήν. οἱ δὲ ἐν τοῖς τιτθοῖς, ὅταν ἔχωσι γάλα, καὶ τῆς ἐκείνου τι γλυκύτητος ἐμφαίνουσι καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν ὑῶν. ἡ δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν τροφὴ, καλῶς μὲν πεφθέντων, ἐγγύς τι τῇ κατὰ τὰς σάρκας ἐστίν, ἐλλιπέστερον δὲ κατεργασθέντων, τὸν ὠμὸν ἢ τὸν φλεγματώδη χυμὸν γεννᾷ, τῶν μὲν οὖν ὑγρῶν ἀδένων τὸν φλεγματώδη, τῶν δὲ σκληροτέρων τὸν ὠμόν.
greek_normalized: παντων αδενων κοινον, ηδεις τε και ψαθυρους φαινεσθαι κατα την εδωδην. οι δε εν τοις τιτθοις, οταν εχωσι γαλα, και της εκεινου τι γλυκυτητος εμφαινουσι και μαλιστα επι των υων. η δε εξ αυτων τροφη, καλως μεν πεφθεντων, εγγυς τι τῃ κατα τας σαρκας εστιν, ελλιπεστερον δε κατεργασθεντων, τον ωμον η τον φλεγματωδη χυμον γεννᾳ, των μεν ουν υγρων αδενων τον φλεγματωδη, των δε σκληροτερων τον ωμον.
translation: About glands. All glands have that in common that they are clearly pleasant and friable to eat. Those in the teats, when they contain milk, also exhibit some of its sweetness, and especially in the case of pigs. The nourishment derived from them, when digested well, is somewhat close to that from meat, but when they are less adequately processed, they produce a crude humour that is apt to produce phlegm: wet glands produce humour apt to produce phlegm, while hard ones produce crude humour.

greek: τῶν ἀδενωδῶν σωμάτων εἰσὶ καὶ οἱ ὄρχεις. οἱ μὲν οὖν τῶν ὑῶν ἢ προβάτων ἢ τράγων ὄρχεις ἐσθιόμενοὶ εἰσι δύσπεπτοι καὶ κακόχυμοι, διὰ τὸ ἐνυπάρχον ἐν αὐτοῖς βρομῶδες. εἰς ὅσον δὲ ἡ τῶν ὑῶν σὰρξ τῆς τῶν ἄλλων ἐστὶ βελτίων, εἰς τοσοῦτον καὶ οἱ ὄρχεις. πεφθέντες δὲ καλῶς τρόφιμοι γίγνονται. μόνοι δὲ οἱ τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων ὄρχεις ἄριστοι κατὰ πάντα καὶ ἥδιστοι καὶ τροφὴν χρηστὴν τῷ σώματι διδόασι, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν σιτευθέντων.
greek_normalized: των αδενωδων σωματων εισι και οι ορχεις. οι μεν ουν των υων η προβατων η τραγων ορχεις εσθιομενοι εισι δυσπεπτοι και κακοχυμοι, δια το ενυπαρχον εν αυτοις βρομωδες. εις οσον δε η των υων σαρξ της των αλλων εστι βελτιων, εις τοσουτον και οι ορχεις. πεφθεντες δε καλως τροφιμοι γιγνονται. μονοι δε οι των αλεκτρυονων ορχεις αριστοι κατα παντα και ηδιστοι και τροφην χρηστην τῳ σωματι διδοασι, και μαλιστα των σιτευθεντων.
translation: Testicles. The testicles, too, belong to the gland-like bodies. Now, the testicles of pigs or sheep or he-goats when eaten are hard to digest and produce bad humours, because of the rank smell present in them. To the extent to which the meat of pigs is better than that of other animals, to that extent their testicles are better, too. If they are digested well, they become nourishing. Only the testicles of cocks are excellent in all respects, and most pleasant, and give good nourishment to the body, and in particular that of cocks that are fattened.

greek: κακόχυμοὶ εἰσι φανερῶς καὶ δύσπεπτοι, ἐμφαίνοντες ἐν τῇ γεύσει καὶ τὴν τοῦ οὔρου ποιότητα.
greek_normalized: κακοχυμοι εισι φανερως και δυσπεπτοι, εμφαινοντες εν τῃ γευσει και την του ουρου ποιοτητα.
translation: Kidneys. They clearly produce bad humours and are hard to digest, displaying also the property of urine in their taste.

greek: φλεγματικώτερόν ἐστιν ἔδεσμα ἐγκέφαλος καὶ παχύχυμον καὶ βραδύπορον καὶ δύσπεπτον, μάλιστα δὲ καὶ κακοστόμαχον ἅπας ἐγκέφαλος. ἐξαπατώμενοι δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς μαλακότητος αὐτοῦ ἔνιοι διδόασιν αὐτὸν τοῖς ἀσθενοῦσιν, ὄντα πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις καὶ ναυτιώδη. μᾶλλον οὖν ὅταν ἐμέσαι τινὰ βουληθείης ἀπὸ τροφῆς καὶ ἐγκέφαλον αὐτῷ δίδου λιπαρῶς ἠρτυμένον ἐν τοῖς τελευταίοις προςενέγκασθαι, φυλάττου δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀνορέκτων. μετὰ δὲ τῶν τεμνόντων καὶ θερμαινόντων σκευασθεὶς βαλτίων ἑαυτοῦ γίγνεται.
greek_normalized: φλεγματικωτερον εστιν εδεσμα εγκεφαλος και παχυχυμον και βραδυπορον και δυσπεπτον, μαλιστα δε και κακοστομαχον απας εγκεφαλος. εξαπατωμενοι δε υπο της μαλακοτητος αυτου ενιοι διδοασιν αυτον τοις ασθενουσιν, οντα προς τοις αλλοις και ναυτιωδη. μαλλον ουν οταν εμεσαι τινα βουληθειης απο τροφης και εγκεφαλον αυτῳ διδου λιπαρως ηρτυμενον εν τοις τελευταιοις προςενεγκασθαι, φυλαττου δε επι των ανορεκτων. μετα δε των τεμνοντων και θερμαινοντων σκευασθεις βαλτιων εαυτου γιγνεται.
translation: About the brain. The brain is a food fairly rich in phlegm, with thick juices, slow-passing and hard to digest, and the whole brain is especially bad for the stomach. Deceived by its softness, some give it to the ailing, while it is also sickening in addition to the other [characteristics]. Rather, then, if you want to make someone vomit after food, give him also brain prepared with fat to force down at the end [of the meal], but be careful with people without an appetite. When prepared with cutting and heating [substances?], it becomes better than it was.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῶν ἐν πεζοῖς ζῴοις σπλάγχνων
greek: τὸ μὲν ἧπαρ πάντων τῶν ζῴων παχύχυμόν ἐστι καὶ δύσπεπτον καὶ βραδύπορον· ἄμεινον δὲ ἐν αὐτοῖς οὐκ εἰς ἡδονὴν μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς τὰ ἄλλα τὸ τῶν σύκοις ξηροῖς σιτευθέντων χοίρων καὶ διὰ τοῦτο συκωτὸν καλούμενον. ὁ δὲ σπλὴν κακόχυμος εἶναι πεπίστευται, μελαγχολικοῦ αἵματος γεννητικὸς ὑπάρχων. ἀμφοῖν δὲ εὐπεπτότερος ὁ πνεύμων, ὅσῳ καὶ ἀραιότερος, εἰς δὲ θρέψιν πάμπολυ τοῦ ἥπατος ἥττων. ἣν οὖν δίδωσι τροφὴν τῷ σώματι, φλεγματικωτέρα μᾶλλόν ἐστι διὰ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ χονδρώδη σώματα τῆς τραχείας ἀρτηρίας· ἡ δὲ καρδία δύσπεπτος καὶ βραδύπορος· εἰ δὲ πεφθείη, τροφὴν οὐκ ὀλίγην, οὐδὲ κακόχυμον δίδωσι τῷ σώματι.
greek_normalized: το μεν ηπαρ παντων των ζῳων παχυχυμον εστι και δυσπεπτον και βραδυπορον· αμεινον δε εν αυτοις ουκ εις ηδονην μονον αλλα και εις τα αλλα το των συκοις ξηροις σιτευθεντων χοιρων και δια τουτο συκωτον καλουμενον. ο δε σπλην κακοχυμος ειναι πεπιστευται, μελαγχολικου αιματος γεννητικος υπαρχων. αμφοιν δε ευπεπτοτερος ο πνευμων, οσῳ και αραιοτερος, εις δε θρεψιν παμπολυ του ηπατος ηττων. ην ουν διδωσι τροφην τῳ σωματι, φλεγματικωτερα μαλλον εστι δια τα εν αυτῳ χονδρωδη σωματα της τραχειας αρτηριας· η δε καρδια δυσπεπτος και βραδυπορος· ει δε πεφθειη, τροφην ουκ ολιγην, ουδε κακοχυμον διδωσι τῳ σωματι.
translation: About the viscera of land animals. The liver of land animals produces thick humours, is hard to digest and slow-passing. Better among these, not only for pleasure, but also for other [purposes], is the liver of young pigs fattened on dry figs, which because of that is called sukōton. The spleen is trustworthily believed to generate bad humours, as it produces ‘melancholic’ blood. Easier to digest than either are the lungs, by as much as they are also of a looser texture, but much inferior to the liver as far as nutrition is concerned. The nutrition they give to the body is rather rich in phlegm because of the cartilaginous bodies of the trachea (‘rough artery’) contained in them. The heart is hard to digest and slow-passing. If it is digested, it gives considerable nourishment, which does not generate bad humours, to the body.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ κοιλίας καὶ ἐντέρων καὶ μήτρας ἐν τοῖς πεζοῖς ζῴοις
greek: κοιλία καὶ μήτρα καὶ ἔντερα τὰ ἐν τοῖς πεζοῖς ζῴοις σκληρότερὰ ἐστι τῶν σαρκῶν· διὸ κἂν καλῶς πεφθῇ, οὐκ ἀκριβὲς αἷμα καὶ ἄμεμπτον, ἀλλὰ ψυχρότερόν τε καὶ ὠμότερον ἐργάζεται.
greek_normalized: κοιλια και μητρα και εντερα τα εν τοις πεζοις ζῳοις σκληροτερα εστι των σαρκων· διο καν καλως πεφθῃ, ουκ ακριβες αιμα και αμεμπτον, αλλα ψυχροτερον τε και ωμοτερον εργαζεται.
translation: About the gut, the intestines and the womb of land animals. In land animals, the gut, the womb and the intestines are harder than the meat. Therefore, even if they are digested well, they do not produce genuine and unobjectionable blood, but rather cold and crude blood.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῆς τῶν ἀγρίων ζῴων σαρκός
greek: ἡ σὰρξ πάντων τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσι διαιτωμένων ἐστὶ σκληροτέρα καὶ πιμελῆς ὀλίγιστον μετέχει· διὸ καὶ ἀπέριττος ἡ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐστι τροφὴ, μᾶλλον τῶν ἡμέρων.
greek_normalized: η σαρξ παντων των εν τοις ορεσι διαιτωμενων εστι σκληροτερα και πιμελης ολιγιστον μετεχει· διο και απεριττος η εξ αυτων εστι τροφη, μαλλον των ημερων.
translation: About the meat of wild animals. The meat of all animals living in the mountains is harder and partakes of very little fat. Therefore, the nourishment derived from them is also without residues, more so than that of domesticated animals.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν πτηνῶν ζῴων τροφῆς
greek: τὸ γένος ἁπάντων τῶν πτηνῶν ζῴων ὀλιγοτροφώτερόν ἐστιν, εἰ παραβάλλοιτο τῷ γένει τῶν πεζῶν, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ὑῶν. εὐπεπτοτέρα γε μὴν ἡ σάρξ ἐστι τῶν πτηνῶν καὶ μάλιστα πέρδικος ἀτταγῆνός τε καὶ περιστερᾶς ἀλεκτορίδος τε καὶ ἀλεκτρυόνος. ἡ δὲ τῶν κιχλῶν καὶ κοσσύφων καὶ τῶν μικρῶν στρουθῶν καὶ τῶν πυργιτῶν σκληροτέρα τούτων ἐστὶ, καὶ μᾶλλον ἔτι τούτων αὐτῶν ἥ τε τῆς τρυγόνος καὶ ἡ τῆς φάττης καὶ τῆς νήσσης· ὁμοία δὲ τῇ τῶν ἀλεκτορίδων ἐστὶν ἡ τῶν φασιανικῶν εἰς πέψιν καὶ τροφήν, ὑπερέχουσα τῇ κατὰ τὴν ἐδωδὴν ἡδονῇ. σκληροτέρα δὲ καὶ δυσπεπτοτέρα τούτων καὶ ἰνωδεστέρα ἡ τοῦ ταώ. κοινὸν δὲ πᾶσι τοῖς πτηνοῖς ζῴοις, ὥσπερ καὶ τοῖς τετράποσι, γινώσκειν χρὴ, τῶν ἔτι αὐξανομένων τὴν σάρκα πολὺ βελτίονα τῆς τῶν ἀκμαζόντων εἶναι, μέσην δὲ ἀμφοῖν τὴν τῶν ἀκμαζόντων, μοχθηρὰν δὲ τὴν τῶν γεγηρακότων καὶ τῶν νηπίων. ἡ μὲν γὰρ τῶν νέων βλεννώδης καὶ ὑγρὰ καὶ περιττωματικὴ καὶ ῥᾷον ὑπέρχεται κατὰ γαστέρα, ἡ δὲ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων σκληρὰ καὶ ξηρὰ καὶ νευρώδης καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πεφθῆναι μοχθηρά. ταῦτὰ μοι μέμνησο καθόλου περὶ πάντων τῶν ζῴων. οὐ σμικρὰ δὲ διαφορὰ καὶ τῶν ἐν λίμναις ἢ ἕλεσιν ἢ τελματώδεσι χωρίοις διαιτωμένων πρὸς τὰ κατ' ὄρη καὶ ξηροὺς τόπους· ἀνάλογον γὰρ τοῖς χωρίοις καὶ αἱ σάρκες τῶν ζῴων ἤτοι ξηραὶ καὶ ἀπέριττοι καὶ πεφθῆναι ῥᾴους, ἢ ὑγραὶ καὶ περιττωματικαὶ καὶ δυσπεπτότεραι γίγνονται.
greek_normalized: το γενος απαντων των πτηνων ζῳων ολιγοτροφωτερον εστιν, ει παραβαλλοιτο τῳ γενει των πεζων, και μαλιστα των υων. ευπεπτοτερα γε μην η σαρξ εστι των πτηνων και μαλιστα περδικος ατταγηνος τε και περιστερας αλεκτοριδος τε και αλεκτρυονος. η δε των κιχλων και κοσσυφων και των μικρων στρουθων και των πυργιτων σκληροτερα τουτων εστι, και μαλλον ετι τουτων αυτων η τε της τρυγονος και η της φαττης και της νησσης· ομοια δε τῃ των αλεκτοριδων εστιν η των φασιανικων εις πεψιν και τροφην, υπερεχουσα τῃ κατα την εδωδην ηδονῃ. σκληροτερα δε και δυσπεπτοτερα τουτων και ινωδεστερα η του ταω. κοινον δε πασι τοις πτηνοις ζῳοις, ωσπερ και τοις τετραποσι, γινωσκειν χρη, των ετι αυξανομενων την σαρκα πολυ βελτιονα της των ακμαζοντων ειναι, μεσην δε αμφοιν την των ακμαζοντων, μοχθηραν δε την των γεγηρακοτων και των νηπιων. η μεν γαρ των νεων βλεννωδης και υγρα και περιττωματικη και ρᾳον υπερχεται κατα γαστερα, η δε των πρεσβυτερων σκληρα και ξηρα και νευρωδης και δια τουτο πεφθηναι μοχθηρα. ταυτα μοι μεμνησο καθολου περι παντων των ζῳων. ου σμικρα δε διαφορα και των εν λιμναις η ελεσιν η τελματωδεσι χωριοις διαιτωμενων προς τα κατ' ορη και ξηρους τοπους· αναλογον γαρ τοις χωριοις και αι σαρκες των ζῳων ητοι ξηραι και απεριττοι και πεφθηναι ρᾳους, η υγραι και περιττωματικαι και δυσπεπτοτεραι γιγνονται.
translation: About nourishment from birds. The whole class of birds is rather poor in nutrition when compared to the order of land animals, and in particular when compared to pigs. The meat of birds is more easily digested, and in particular that of the partridge, the francolin, the dove, the hen and the cock. The meat of thrushes and blackbirds and small house-sparrows and sparrows is harder than the former, and even harder than these, is that of the turtledove, the ringdove and the duck. The meat of pheasants is similar to that of hens for digestion and nourishment, whilst being superior for the pleasure in eating. The meat of the peacock is harder, and harder to digest, and more sinewy than the above. In common for all birds - as also for all four-legged animals - one needs to know that the meat of those that are still growing is much better than that of those past their prime, with that of animals in their prime being halfway between the two, and that of aged animals and of the very young both being bad. For meat of very young animals is slimy and wet and full of residues, and it passes easily in the stomach, while that of older animals is hard and sinewy, and therefore is not well digested. Keep this in mind about all animals in general. The difference between animals living in marshes and swampy areas and those living in mountains and dry places is considerable. For by the same rationale as for places, the meat of the animals, too, becomes either dry and without residues and easy to digest, or wet and full of residues and harder to digest.

greek: περιττωματικὴ τούτων ἡ σάρξ ἐστι καὶ δυσπεπτοτέρα τῆς τῶν εἰρημένων πτηνῶν, οὐ μὴν τὰ γε πτερὰ χείρω τῶν εἰρημένων ἔχει.
greek_normalized: περιττωματικη τουτων η σαρξ εστι και δυσπεπτοτερα της των ειρημενων πτηνων, ου μην τα γε πτερα χειρω των ειρημενων εχει.
translation: About wild geese and ostriches. The meat of these is full of residues and harder to digest than that of the aforementioned, but their wings are no worse than the aforementioned.

greek: ἡ δὲ τῶν γεράνων σὰρξ ὅλη σκληρὰ καὶ ἰνώδης, πολλῷ δὲ μᾶλλον τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῶν σκληρότερα τὰ πτερά.
greek_normalized: η δε των γερανων σαρξ ολη σκληρα και ινωδης, πολλῳ δε μαλλον της σαρκος αυτων σκληροτερα τα πτερα.
translation: About cranes. The meat of cranes is all hard and sinewy, and the wings are much harder than [the rest of] their meat.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῆς κατὰ τὰ μόρια τῶν πτηνῶν ζῴων διαφορᾶς
greek: τὰ μὲν σπλάγχνα τὴν αὐτὴν ἀναλογίαν ἔχει πρὸς τὰς σάρκας καὶ ἐν τοῖς πτηνοῖς ζῴοις, ἣν καὶ ἐν τοῖς πεζοῖς ἔχειν εἴρηται. τὰ δ' ἔντερα ἄβρωτα σχεδὸν πάντων αὐτῶν ἐστιν. αἱ δὲ γαστέρες αὐτῶν ἐδώδιμοὶ τὲ εἰσι καὶ τρόφιμοι καὶ τινες αὐτῶν καὶ ἡδεῖαι, καθάπερ ἡ τῶν χηνῶν, ἐφεξῆς δ' ἡ τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων. ἐπαινοῦσι δὲ ἔνιοι ψευδῶς τὴν τοῦ στρουθοκαμήλου κοιλίαν, ὥς τι φάρμακον πεπτικόν, ἔνιοι δὲ πολὺ μᾶλλον τῆσδε τὴν τῆς αἰθυίας γαστέρα θαυμάζουσιν· ἀλλ' οὔτε αὗται πέττονται ῥᾳδίως, οὔτε τῶν ἄλλων σιτίων εἰσὶ πεπτικὸν φάρμακον. τὰ δὲ πτερὰ κάλλιστα μὲν τὰ τῶν εὐτρόφων καὶ νέων, χείριστα δὲ τὰ τῶν ἰσχνῶν καὶ γεγηρακότων. οἱ δὲ ὄρχεις ἄριστοι, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν σιτευθέντων ἀλεκτρυόνων, ἔτι δὲ μᾶλλον τῶν διὰ γάλακτος ὀρροῦ τὰς τροφὰς προσενεγκαμένων· καὶ γὰρ εὔχυμοι καὶ τρόφιμοι καὶ πεφθῆναι ῥᾷστοι. διαχώρησιν δὲ οὔτε προτρέπουσιν οὔτε ἐπέχουσιν. ἐγκεφάλους δὲ βελτίονας ἔχει πολλῷ τὰ πτηνὰ ζῷα τῶν ἐν τοῖς πεζοῖς, ὅσῳ καὶ ξηροτέρους καὶ μάλιστα τῶν ὀρείων ὀρνίθων.

translation: About the difference according to the parts of the winged animals. In the winged animals, too, the viscera have the same relation to the meat as has been described in the land animals. The intestines of nearly all of them are inedible. Their stomachs are edible and nourishing, and some of them are even pleasant [to eat], such as those of wild geese, followed by those of cocks. Some wrongly praise the intestine of the ostrich as some remedy that promotes digestion, and some admire much more the stomach of the shearwater, but neither of these are easily digested themselves, nor are they a remedy promoting digestion of other foodstuffs. As for the wings, the best are those of well-nourished and young animals, while the worst are those of lean and aged ones. The testicles are best, especially those of fattened cocks, and even more so those of cocks fed with milk whey, for they are apt to produce good humours, and are nourishing and the easiest to digest. They neither stimulate nor hinder excretions. Winged animals have far better brains than those found in land animals, to the extent that they are also drier, and especially those of mountain birds.

greek: ὠὰ ἀμείνω τὰ τε τῶν ἀλεκτορίδων ἐστὶ καὶ τῶν φασιανῶν, φαυλότερα δὲ τὰ τῶν χηνῶν καὶ στρουθοκαμήλων. κάλλιστα μὲν οὖν εἰς τροφὴν τοῦ σώματός ἐστι τὰ τρομητὰ καλούμενα, τὰ δὲ ῥοφητὰ ἧττον μὲν τρέφει, ῥᾷον δὲ ὑποχωρεῖ. τὰς δὲ ἐν τῷ φάρυγγι τραχύτητας διὰ κραυγὴν ἢ χυμοῦ δριμύτητα ἐκλεαίνει, περιπλαττόμενα τοῖς πεπονθόσι τόποις καὶ προσμένοντα ὥσπερ τι κατάπλασμα καὶ τῷ τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ἀδήκτῳ ἐκθεραπεύοντα καὶ τὰς τραχύτητας. τῷ δὲ αὐτῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὰς κατὰ τὸν στόμαχον καὶ γαστέρα καὶ κύστιν ἰᾶται τραχύτητας· ἐν ὄξει δὲ ἑψηθὲν ὠὸν εἰ βρωθείη, ξηραίνει τὰ κατὰ γαστέρα ῥεύματα. καὶ εἰ μίξας δὲ αὐτῷ τι τῶν πρὸς δυσεντερίαν ἢ κοιλιακὴν διάθεσιν ἁρμοττόντων, εἶτα ἐπ' ἀνθράκων ταγηνίσας, δοίης φαγεῖν, οὐ σμικρὰ τοὺς κάμνοντας ὠφελήσεις. ἐπιτήδεια δὲ ἐστιν εἰς ταῦτα ὀμφάκιον καὶ ῥοῦς ἐπιπαττόμενος καὶ τέφρα τῶν κοχλιῶν ὅλων καέντων γίγαρτὰ τε σταφυλῆς καὶ μύρτα καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια. τὰ δὲ ἑφθὰ ὠὰ δύσπεπτα καὶ βραδύπορα καὶ τροφὴν παχεῖαν ἀναδίδωσι τῷ σώματι. τούτων δὲ ἔτι μᾶλλον βραδυπορώτερὰ τε καὶ παχυχυμότερα τὰ κατὰ θερμὴν σποδιὰν ὀπτηθέντα. τὰ δὲ ταγηνισθέντα χειρίστην ἔχει τροφὴν εἰς ἅπαντα· καὶ γὰρ ἐν τῷ πέττεσθαι κνισσοῦται καὶ παχὺν χυμὸν γεννᾷ καὶ μοχθηρὸν καὶ περιττωματικόν. ἀμείνω δὲ τῶν ἑφθῶν τε καὶ ὀπτῶν ἐστι τὰ καλούμενα πηκτὰ μετ' ἐλαίου καὶ γάρου καὶ οἴνου βραχέος ἀναδευθέντα καὶ ἐπὶ διπλώματος ἑψηθέντα μέχρι μετρίας συστάσεως. τὰ γὰρ ἐπὶ πλέον παχυνθέντα παραπλήσια τοῖς ἑψηθεῖσι καὶ ὀπτηθεῖσι γίγνεται. τὸ αὐτὸ δὲ χρὴ ποιεῖν κἀπὶ τῶν ἐπιχεομένων ταῖς λοπάσιν ὠῶν, ἔτι ἐγχύλων ὄντων ἀπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς αἴροντας τὴν λοπάδα.

translation: About eggs. The better ones are those of hens and of pheasants, and those of wild geese and ostriches are less good. Now, those called tromēta are best for nourishment. Runny ones nourish less, but are passed more easily. They smoothe away roughness in the fauces that results from shouting or from the sharpness of a humour when plastered on to the affected places and left in place like some poultice. And they also cure rough patches by the fact that their entire essence is non-stinging. By the same rationale they also heal rough patches in the stomach and the bladder. If an egg is boiled in vinegar and eaten, it dries the fluxes in the stomach. And if you mix it with one of the remedies fitting for dysentery or a disposition with bowel problems, then broil it on coals and give it to eat, you will benefit the patients to no small extent. Suitable remedies for this are the juice of unripe grapes, and sumach (plastered on), and the ash of burnt entire snails, as well as grape pips and myrtle-berries and the like. Boiled eggs are hard to digest and slow-passing, and they provide thick nourishment for the body. Eggs that are baked in hot ashes are even more slow-passing and productive of thick/dense humours than these. Broiled ones have the least good nutrition for everything. For they become greasy in the course of coction, and generate a thick humour that is bad and full of residues. Better than the boiled and baked ones are the so-called ‘congealed’ (pēkta) eggs, briefly soaked in oil or garum and wine and boiled on a double pot until they reach medium consistency. For eggs that are thickened over a longer time become similar to boiled or baked ones. One needs to do the same with eggs that are poured on to a flat pan (lopas), by taking the pan off the fire while they are still runny.

greek: ὅσα ὡς φάρμακον ἐνεργεῖται ὠά. Ἐπὶ δυσεντερικῶν καὶ κοιλιακῶν διαθέσεων διδόμενον τὸ ὠὸν τῷ προειρημένῳ τρόπῳ ἄριστον φάρμακον τῷ πάθει γίγνεται. τὸ δὲ λευκὸν καὶ λεπτὸν τῶν προσφάτων ὠῶν ἀδηκτότατόν ἐστι φάρμακον οὐ μόνον ἐπ' ὀφθαλμῶν προςαγόμενον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ὅσα τῶν ἀδηκτοτάτων δεῖται φαρμάκων, ὡς τὰ καθ' ἕδραν τε καὶ τὰ αἰδοῖα ἕλκη καὶ τὰ κακοήθη πάντα. <καὶ πρὸς τὰ κακοήθη δὲ> τοῖς ξηραίνειν ἀδήκτως αὐτὰ πεφυκόσι μίγνυται, ὁποῖός ἐστιν ὅ τε πομφόλυξ καὶ τὰ ὅμοια. ἐστὶ δὲ καὶ ἡ λέκιθος ὁμοίας δυνάμεως καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μίγνυται κηρωταῖς ἀδήκτοις, ἑψηθέντων ἢ ὀπτηθέντων τῶν ὠῶν. ὅσῳ δὲ ξηρότερα γέγονε, τοσοῦτον ἀπόλλυσι τοῦ παρηγορικοῦ. τὰ δὲ ὄστρακα τῶν ὠῶν καυθέντα ἴσχαιμον γίγνεται φάρμακον.

translation: Eggs that have an effect as a remedy. In the case of dysentery and bowel conditions, eggs given in the way described above become an excellent remedy for the affection. The thin egg-white of fresh eggs is a most sting-free remedy, not only when applied to the eyes, but also to all the other [parts] that need most sting-free remedies, such as ulcers in the anus and the genitals, and all the malignant ones. <And for the malignant ones,> it is mixed with [substances] that by nature dry without stinging, such as zinc oxide and similar ones. The yolk, too, has a similar capacity, and because of that it is mixed into sting-free cerates, the eggs having been boiled or baked. The drier it becomes, the more it loses its soothing quality. Burnt eggshells become a haemostatic remedy.

chapter_title_gr: περὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐνύδρων ζῴων τροφῆς
greek: τῶν ἐν ὕδατι διαιτωμένων ζῴων καὶ γένη πάμπολλα καὶ εἴδη τούτων εἰσὶ καὶ διαφοραί. λεχθήσεται δὲ νῦν, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ἔμπροσθεν, ὅσα πρὸς τὴν ἰατρικὴν ἢ ὑγιεινὴν χρείαν ἐξ αὐτῶν παραλαμβάνεται. καθόλου τοίνυν χρὴ γιγνώσκειν ὡς καλλίστη σάρξ ἐστιν ἰχθύων τῶν ἐν καθαρᾷ θαλάττῃ διαιτωμένων, καὶ μᾶλλον ὅταν ὑπὸ ἀνέμων καταιγίζηται ὁ τόπος καὶ μήτε γεώδεις αἰγιαλοὶ μήτε λεῖοι περιλαμβάνουσι τὸ ὕδωρ, ἀλλ' ἤτοι ψαμμώδεις ἢ τραχεῖς καὶ λιθώδεις· εἰ δὲ καὶ πρὸς τὰ βόρεια τῶν πνευμάτων εἶεν οἱ τόποι ἐστραμμένοι, πολὺ βέλτιον. πρόδηλον δὲ ὡς καὶ θάλαττα θαλάττης ἀμείνων ἐστὶ καθόσον ἤτοι καθαρὰ τελέως ἐστίν, ἢ δέχεται ποταμοὺς μεγάλους τε καὶ πολλούς. οἵ τε γὰρ ἐν τῇ τοιαύτῃ θαλάττῃ διαιτώμενοι ἰχθύες, καθ' ὅσον πλεονεκτοῦσι τῶν λιμναίων, κατὰ τοσοῦτον ἀπολείπονται τῶν ἐν τῇ καθαρᾷ θαλάττῃ διαιτωμένων. καὶ γὰρ καὶ οἱ κατὰ τὴν σκεπινὴν καὶ ἀκύμονα θάλατταν διαιτώμενοι χείρονα τὴν σάρκα κέκτηνται. τῶν δὲ ἐν ταῖς λιμνοθαλάτταις διαιτωμένων ἰχθύων ἡ σὰρξ μεταξὺ πως τῶν ποταμίων καὶ τῶν θαλαττίων γίγνεται. περιττωματικὴ δὲ σάρξ ἐστι καὶ βλεννώδης ἱκανῶς τῶν ἐν ἰλυώδει καὶ ῥυπαρῷ ὕδατι διαιτωμένων, ἔτι δὲ χείρων τῆσδε καὶ ἡ τῶν ἐν λίμναις διαιτωμένων σάρξ. εἰ δὲ καὶ σμικραὶ τινες αἱ λίμναι τύχοιεν οὖσαι καὶ μήτε ποταμοὺς μεγάλους δεχόμεναι μήτε πηγὴν ἔχουσαι μήτε ἀπορροὴν δαψιλῆ πολὺ δήτι χείρους· εἰ δὲ μηδόλως ἀπορρεῖ τι τοῦ ὕδατος ἀλλ' εἴη στάσιμον ἱκανῶς μοχθηραί. τῶν δὲ ἐν ἕλεσι καὶ τέλμασι καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα χωρία διαιτωμένων, ἐσχάτως μοχθηρὰ καὶ ἡ σάρξ· τῶν δὲ ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γεννωμένων ἀμείνους, οἱ κατὰ τοὺς τοιούτους ποταμούς, ἐν οἷς ὀξὺ καὶ πολὺ τὸ ῥεῦμα. τῶν δὲ κατὰ τοὺς λιμνάζοντας ποταμοὺς ἰχθύων ἡ σὰρξ οὐκ ἀγαθὴ πεφθῆναι καὶ τὴν μὲν χρηστὴν τροφὴν ὀλιγίστην ἔχουσι. καὶ χείριστοι δὲ γίγνονται οἱ κατὰ τὰς ἐκβολὰς τῶν ποταμῶν, ὅσοι κοπρῶνας ἐκκαθαίρουσιν ἢ βαλανεῖα ἢ μαγειρεῖα καὶ τὸν τῆς ἐσθῆτός τε καὶ τῶν ὀθονῶν ῥύπον, ὅσα τε ἄλλα τῆς πόλεως ἐστὶ, ἣν παραρρέουσι καθάρσεως δεόμενα, καὶ μάλισθ' ὅταν ᾖ πολυάνθρωπος ἡ πόλις. καὶ παρὰ τὰς τροφὰς δὲ βελτίους γίγνονται καὶ χείρους. ἔνιοι μὲν γὰρ εὐποροῦσι καὶ πόας καὶ ῥιζῶν χρηστῶν, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο κρείττους εἰσί· ἔνιοι δὲ ἰλυώδη τε πόαν ἐσθίουσι καὶ ῥίζας κακοχύμους καὶ τινες αὐτῶν ὅσοι κατὰ ποταμοὺς διαιτῶνται, μεγάλην διαρρέοντας πόλιν, ἀποπατήματα ἀνθρώπων καὶ τινας τοιαύτας προσφέρονται μοχθηρὰς τροφάς. χείριστοι δὲ οὗτοι, ὡς ἔφην, εἰσὶ κἂν βραχὺ πλείονι χρόνῳ διαμείνωσι μετὰ τὴν θήραν σήπονται παραχρῆμα, καὶ μοχθηρότατον ὄζουσιν. ἀηδεῖς δὲ καὶ βρωθῆναι πάντες οὗτοι καὶ πεφθῆναι καὶ τὴν μὲν χρηστὴν τροφὴν ὀλιγίστην ἔχουσι, περίττωμα δὲ οὐκ ὀλίγον καὶ κακοχυμίαν ἀθροίζουσιν ἐν τοῖς σώμασι τῶν ὁσημέραι προςφερομένων αὐτούς.

And if the areas should also be agitated by the north winds, it would be much better. And it is obvious that one sea is better than another according to whether it is either perfectly clean or whether it receives many large rivers. For the fish living in the latter kind of sea are inferior to those living in a clean sea to the extent to which they resemble fish in lakes. And indeed, those living in a sheltered sea that is also not agitated by waves have less good flesh. The flesh of fish living in lagoons is halfway between that of river fish and that of sea fish. The flesh of those living in muddy and dirty water is full of residues and slimy, and the flesh of those living in lakes is even worse. If the lakes also happen to be small and neither receive large rivers nor do they have a spring or an abundant outflow, they are indeed much worse. If absolutely none of the water runs off, but it is stagnant, they are excessively bad. The flesh of fish living in marshes and swamps and any places of that kind is bad to the extreme. Of the fish in rivers, those are better that are in rivers in which the current is swift and strong. The flesh of fish in rivers that form stagnant pools is not good to digest, and they have very little good nourishment. And according to their nourishment the fish also become either better or worse. For some find plenty of good grasses and roots, and because of that are stronger, while others eat muddy grass and roots that generate bad humours, and some of them - those who live in rivers that flow through a large city - eat human excrement and other bad foods of that kind. These, as I said, are the worst, and if they are left a little while longer after being caught, they rot immediately, and they smell extremely bad. All these are unpleasant to eat and to digest and have very little good nourishment, and they accumulate a considerable amount of residue and a bad state of humours in the bodies of those who partake of them every day.

greek: οὐ σμικρὰ διαφορὰ τῶν σαρκῶν ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ταριχεύεσθαὶ τινας τούτων. ὅλῳ γὰρ τῷ παντὶ διαλλάττουσιν, ὡς πολλάκις ὑγροῦ τῇ κράσει ζῴου ταριχευθεῖσαν σάρκα ξηραντικωτέραν εἶναι μακρῷ τῆς φύσει ξηρᾶς ἀταριχεύτου. ἐπιτήδεια μὲν οὖν ἐστι πρὸς ταριχείαν σώματα ζῴων, ὅσα σκληράς τε ἅμα καὶ περιττωματικὰς ἔχει τὰς σάρκας. τὰ δὲ ἤτοι πάνυ μαλακὴν ἢ πάνυ ξηρὰν καὶ ἀπέριττον ἔχοντα τὴν ἕξιν τοῦ σώματος οὐκ ἐπιτήδεια ταριχεύεσθαι. ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ ξηρὰ σώματα βύρσαις ὅμοια γίγνεται ταριχευθέντα, οὕτως ὅσα λίαν ὑγρὰ διαρρεῖ καὶ τήκεται τοῖς ἁλσὶν ὁμιλοῦντα. πρόδηλον οὖν ὡς ὅσα σκληρὰ καὶ νευρώδη καὶ οἱονεὶ δερματώδη καὶ βυρσώδη, ταριχευθέντα γίγνεται δύσπεπτα πάντα. τὰ δ' εὔθετα εἰς ταριχείαν λεπτομερῆ γίγνεται καὶ λεπτύνει ἐσθιόμενα τοὺς παχεῖς καὶ κολλώδεις χυμούς. τὰ δὲ παλαιὰ πάντα ταρίχη μοχθηρά.

translation: About all cured [flesh of] animals - terrestrial, winged and aquatic. There is a considerable difference between the kinds of flesh when some of these are preserved. For they change in their entirety, so that often the cured flesh of an animal that is of a wet mixture is drier by far than uncured flesh that is dry by nature. Now, the bodies of those animals are suitable for preservation that have hard flesh which is full of residues. The animals whose bodily condition is either altogether soft, or altogether dry and without residues, are not suitable for preservation. Just as dry bodies become like hide when cured, those that are excessively wet waste away and melt when they come into contact with the salts. It is obvious, then, that those that are hard and sinewy, as it were skin-like and hide-like, all become hard to digest when cured. Those that are well-adapted to preservation become fine-particled and, when eaten, comminute thick and glutinous humours. Old cured [foodstuffs] are all bad.

translation: About brine. The brine of salted fish is fitting for ulcers inclined to putrefy and, as an enema, for hip problems and dysentery, in the same way as garum. For because of its sharpness it attracts the humours/juices that cause trouble to the hip and evacuates them through the intestines, and it washes out and dries the ulcers that are inclined to putrefy in dysentery. translation: About hard and soft fat/lard and suet?. The capacity of all soft fat is moistening and heating for human bodies. The variety in each of them is a matter of more or less. Soft fat differs from thick fat by its thickness, and therefore hard fat is formed in animals that have a rather earthy nature overall, just as soft fat is formed in those that have a wetter nature. For that very reason soft fat melts easily on the fire, but it does not congeal easily. Hard fat, on the other hand, does not melt easily, and if it does melt, it is much harder in appearance than soft fat. The lard of pigs is nearly the wettest/most liquid of all; it is more softening and more digestive than oil, and because of that it is mixed into poultices for inflammations. For those who have an irritation/a stinging pain of the rectum or the colon, and for those suffering from dysentery and the vain urge to evacuate, we rather inject goats’ suet - not because it takes the edge off the sharpness, but because it congeals easily because of its thickness. For pigs’ lard runs off like oil. Goose fat is hotter than that of pigs, but it is also altogether made of fine particles, and because of that we inject it in the case of those who have an irritation/biting in the depth of the body. For because of its fineness it penetrates the entire body and mingles with the biting/stinging juices/humours, and takes the edge off/dulls the irritation. The fat of cocks and hens is in between that of pigs and that of geese. That of bulls is much hotter and drier than pigs’ lard. That of calves falls short of that of bulls regarding the hotness and dryness, and in the same way the fat of kids falls short of that of goats and he-goats. Again, the fat of he-goats falls short of that of lions; for that of lions is pretty much the most dispersive and has the finest particles of all quadrupeds’, wherefore it is most dispersive when applied to chronic, indurated tumescences and stiff joints. Bulls’ fat is situated halfway between that of pigs and that of lions,, and because of that it is mixed with two kinds of remedies: those that treat what is indurated and those that concoct what is inflamed, such as the ones called ‘four-remedy’ (tetrapharmakon) and ‘royal’ (basilikon). Some say that the fat of vipers is fitting for incipient cataracts. It has been written truthfully that bear fat is fitting for alopecia. And some praise fish fat for cataracts and earaches, and they say that the fat of any fish can do these things. With time all fat becomes hotter and more fine-particled than it originally was, and therefore more dispersive. This is the case with all [fats?] that are left for some time, at least those that do not become corrupted first. It is a point that is common for this discussion - which one needs to keep in mind - that according to the mixture of animals there always occur varieties of the fat in them, and that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the gelded male is the same as the female, just as any young animal is. Thus also the wild animal is better than the domesticated one.

translation: About foxes. They treat those suffering from joint pain by boiling some foxes alive in oil. They fill tubs with the warm oil and make those suffering from joint pain immerge their entire bodies in these, enjoining them to stay in them for a long time. Oil of this kind becomes dispersive, drawing to the surface all that is contained in the body and causes the pain there - either by the thickness of the essence, or by chilling, or strong sharpness, or windy pneuma that does not have an exit. For because of this it occurs that not only the tumescences on the joints are emptied, but also the entire body (being in a plerotic condition), and that because of that there follows great succour/benefit, as the causes contained in the joints are dispersed, nothing new runs on to the affected parts, and the entire body becomes free from superfluity. To those who are careless about their regimen, the affection returns, but not as strong as before. For before it was the bad regimen that caused the affection, while the body was sound. Hyena boiled whole in oil does the same as the boiled fox.

translation: About earthworms. Ground earthworms, applied even on severed nerves, help immediately in an amazing way. And they agglutinate every wound made by iron, or stone, or something else, and especially in the nerve-like parts that are hard to agglutinate, such as the nose, or the ear, or the like. One must grind them with the earth in which they are found, unless it partakes of/has some sharp or salty quality. Five or six earthworms, swallowed with grape-syrup, stimulate urination and expell any kind of intestinal worms when drunk in the same way, or however you want. It expels flat intestinal worms when drunk with oxumeli. And six earthworms swallowed in the same way with grape-syrup, purge hard-to-heal jaundice through the urine, both on their own and with trōglitis myrrh of the size of a chickpea; use with confidence. Boiled in rose oil, they assuage earaches, when the warm oil is instilled. It has to be 6 drachms of earthworms and one litra of rose oil. They also cure toothache when the warm oil is instilled into the ear opposite the aching tooth. And when used as a fumigation on coals, they stop toothache, if the patient receives the smoke on the aching tooth through a funnel. Burnt and ground, and sprinkled in a circle around the aching tooth, they remove a molar that needs extracting without a tooth forceps, but one must carefully detach it from the gums all around in advance. The very fine ash of earthworms burnt completely on a potsherd, when applied as a dry kollurion, is greatly beneficial for incipient cataract, and helps with eyelids suffering from trichiasis if we have plucked out the remaining hairs in advance and then spread the ash on the areas with a probe. For it prevents the regrowth of the unnatural hairs. When 6 are swallowed, ground, with oinomeli, on an empty stomach for several days, they crush the stones in the bladder, and lead to them being passed in the urine in a short while. They cause abscessions on the inside to break, and dispose one who has swallowed 7 or 9 - according to [the person’s] strength - ground, in 3 kuathoi of water, towards excretion. And they loosen the hardening of nerves that one calls ganglia, when applied as a poultice, ground on their own, and they also check abscessions on the breasts when applied as a poultice on their own. translation: About the viper. The flesh of the viper heats and dries manifesly when eaten. Having cut off the head and the tail, one must skin it and remove all the entrails, and wash the flesh changing the water three times. Then boil like an eel with water and leek and some dill and with a commensurate amount of oil. When the flesh has been boiled, season with a commensurate amount of salt and give to eat, and the sud to sup. That the flesh of the viper cleanses the entire body through the skin when eaten this way, is possible for you to discern from what I experienced while still young. A man suffering from what is called elephas was hideous to look at and foul-smelling. He built a hut near the village, then, and spent time in it. Wine was brought in a jug to some reapers who were harvesting near him, but when the time came for drinking it, when they poured out the wine into a mixing-bowl, a small viper fell out with it. Therefore - from kindness, I suppose - they gave all the wine to the man ailing with elephas, judging it better that he die than that he live. But he, having drunk the wine, became healthy in an amazing way. For his entire tuberous skin fell off, like the shell of an oyster. What was left appeared extremely soft, like the skin of crayfish and crabs when their shell has fallen off. And something like this happened to many others, and the ancients in our parts have recorded it. And we, too, saw many healed by means of vipers, which is why we also mix them into the theriac.

translation: The hedgehog. The flesh of the hedgehog, dried and swallowed, helps in a short time those suffering from elephas, those in a bad bodily condition and those suffering from convulsions or kidney problems, and furthermore those afflicted by dropsy throughout the flesh. For its capacity is dispersive and drying. And its liver, too, dried in the sun and swallowed, altogether helps those suffering from elephas. When burnt, the ash of both, the sea urchin and the hedgehog, is of a detergent, cleansing and dispersive capacity. It therefore also cleanses ulcers that grow proud flesh, and it reduces everything and clears up what is dirty. The ash of a burnt hedgehog, mixed with raw pitch, delivers from alōpekia. When its ash is drunk with oinomeli, it cures kidneys affected by stones and dropsy throughout the flesh. One drinks as much as half of a kochliarion of the ash. The hedgehog is a deliverer from all [kinds of] difficult micturition, from whatever cause it may arise, if its entrails are used as a fumigation under the patient, while he is covered all around everywhere; for it quickly puts an end to the affection. One must salt and dry the entrails and store them, but if there are none available, use the dried flesh or the skin as a fumigation. The entrails provoke a large quantity of urine when as much as a pinch, dry and ground, is swallowed with wine. Its head, burnt and smeared on with bear fat, is not just a cure for alōpekia, but it can also make hair grow from scars. Its skin, burnt and smeared on with fat, especially bear’s fat, heals alōpekia. When the entire hedgehog is boiled down in oil alive, on a gentle fire for a very long time, the oil from it, used to anoint, cures long-standing pain in the hips. A depilatory is also made from it in this way: Put the live hedgehog into an earthen pot holding 12 xestai, with a very thick lid, pour on just 6 xestai of oil, smear the opening of the pot with chalk so that there is no outlet anywhere, and place it directly in the sun during the heat at the time of the Dog Star, for 40 days. Then open and stir carefully with a new ladle. Then strain through strips of cloth and use. Smear on the places [you want to depilate] in the sun and rub for a long time until they are sweating. Then pour on sweet water and wash off. Be careful not to touch other places that do not need depilating.

greek: καρκίνους ποταμίους ὠμοὺς τρίψας καὶ μίξας γάλακτι δίδου πίνειν, καὶ θεραπεύσεις παντὸς ἑρπετοῦ δῆγμα καὶ μάλιστα σκορπίου πληγὴν ἰάσῃ καὶ τὸν ἀπολλύμενον ὑπὸ λαγωοῦ θαλαττίου πόσεως ὀξέως θεραπεύει. δῆλον δὲ ὅτι τὴν ἔνδον αὐτοῦ σάρκα λειοῦν προσήκει σὺν τῷ γάλακτι. βοηθοῦσι δὲ ὁμοίως διδόμενοι καὶ τοῖς φθισικοῖς καὶ ἑψόμενοι ἐν λευκῷ ζωμῷ καὶ ἐσθιόμενοι ἐπιρροφουμένου τοῦ ζωμοῦ. ἥ γε μὴν τέφρα τοῦ κεκαυμένου καρκίνου ξηραντικὴ ὁμοίως τοῖς ἄλλοις καιομένοις, ἰδιότητι δὲ τινι τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας θαυμαστῶς ἐπὶ τῶν λυσσοδήκτων ἐνεργεῖ, καὶ μόνη μέν, ἀλλὰ καὶ μετὰ γεντιανῆς καὶ λιβάνου πολὺ μᾶλλον· εἶναι δὲ χρὴ τοῦ μὲν λιβάνου μίαν μοῖραν, <ε> δὲ τῆς γεντιανῆς καὶ τῆς τέφρας τῶν καρκίνων μοίρας <ι>. καὶ ἄλλως μὲν οὖν καυθεῖσιν ἐχρησάμεθὰ ποτε, ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ δὲ καθ' ὃν ὁ ἡμέτερος διδάσκαλος ἐχρῆτο. ἦν δὲ λοπὰς ἐρυθροῦ χαλκοῦ, καθ' ἣν ἐπιθεὶς ζῶντας τοὺς καρκίνους ὑπέκαιε ξύλοις ἀμπελίνοις μάλιστα ἄχρις οὗ τεφρωθῶσιν, ὡς εὐκόλως λειοῦσθαι. οὕτως εἶχεν ἀεὶ ἕτοιμον παρεσκευασμένον ἐπὶ τῆς οἰκίας τὸ φάρμακον, ὥρᾳ θέρους καίων τοὺς καρκίνους αὐτοὺς τῷ μηνὶ Αὐγούστῳ ἐν τοῖς ὑπὸ κύνα καύμασιν ὀκτωκαιδεκαταίας οὔσης τῆς σελήνης. πίνειν δὲ καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐδίδου τὸ φάρμακον τοῖς λυσσοδήκτοις ἄχρι τῆς τεσσαρακοστῆς ἡμέρας ἐπιπάττων ὕδατι κοχλιάριον εὐμέγεθες. εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀλλὰ μετὰ ἡμέρας τινὰς τοῦ δηχθῆναι προὐνοεῖτο τοῦ δεδηγμένου, δύο κοχλιάρια καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἐδίδου, ὡς ἀναπληρωθῆναι τὰς <μ> δόσεις. ἐχρῆτο δὲ καὶ κατ' αὐτοῦ τοῦ τραύματος τῷ διὰ τῆς Βρυτίας πίσσης φαρμάκῳ, μίαν μὲν λαμβάνων τῆς πίσσης λίτραν, ὄξους δὲ δριμυτάτου <α> ξέστην, ὀποπάνακος δὲ 𐆄 <Γ>. καρκίνου ποταμίου κεκαυμένου τέφραν μέλιτι ἀναβρέξας, ἰάσῃ μὲν ἴχνη ὑπὸ κρύους ῥαγέντα. καὶ δακτύλων ῥαγάδας, ἰάσῃ δὲ καὶ τὰ κακοήθη καὶ καρκινώδη ἕλκη.

translation: River crabs. Triturate raw river crabs, mix them with milk and give them to drink, and you will treat the bite of every snake, and you will especially heal the sting of the scorpion, and it quickly treats one who is on the point of dying from having ingested sea-hare. It is clear that it is appropriate to triturate the flesh inside it with the milk. They help in the same way when given also to the consumptive, both boiled in white broth and eaten, with the broth drunk afterwards. The ash of burnt river crab is drying in the same way as other burnt things are, and by some peculiarity of its entire essence it is marvellously effective on its own, too, in the case of people bitten by a rabid dog, but even more so [when combined] with gentian and frankincense. It needs to be 1 part of frankincense, 5 of gentian and 10 parts of the ash of crabs. And we also use burnt ones in other ways sometimes, generally in the way in which our teacher used them. It was a frying-pan of red copper, on which he placed the crabs alive and burnt them by applying fire from below, mainly with vine twigs, until they were burnt to ashes, so that they could easily be triturated/ground. Thus he always had the remedy ready, prepared, at home, burning those crabs in the summer season, in the month of August, during the heat at the time of the Dog Star, when the moon was at the 18th day. He gave the remedy to drink every day to those who had been bitten by a rabid dog, until the 40th day, sprinkling a good-sized spoonful upon water. If he did not treat the one who had been bitten from the beginning, but after some days, he gave two spoonfuls every day, so as to make up the 40 doses. He also used, on the wound itself, the remedy with Bruttian pitch, taking one litra of the pitch, 1 xestēs of the sharpest vinegar and 3 ounkiai of Hercules’ woundwort. If you mix the ash of burnt river crabs with honey, you will heal soles cracked by the cold and fissures of the fingers, and you will heal even malignant and cancerous ulcers.

greek: καράβου ὄστρακον καύσας καὶ λειώσας δίδου πίνειν μετ' ἀκράτου καὶ παύσεις τὴν κάτω κοιλίαν ῥευματιζομένην. ἐκκαθαίρει δὲ καὶ λιθιῶντας νεφρούς, ψαμμώδη οὖρα πολλὰ ἄγον.

translation: About crayfish. Give the shell of the crayfish, burnt and triturated, to drink with unmixed wine, and you will check a lower digestive tract suffering from flux. It cleanses out even kidneys afflicted by stones, bringing on much urine with sandy sediment.

greek: κάστορος ὄρχεις ὀνομάζουσι καστόριον, ἔνδοξόν τε καὶ πολύχρηστον φάρμακον. ἐνταῦθα δὲ τὴν καθ' ὅλου αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐροῦμεν, πρὸς ἣν ἀποβλέπων τις εὑρίσκειν ἑαυτῷ δυνήσεται τὰς κατὰ μέρος χρήσεις. θερμαίνει δὲ καὶ ξηραίνει, ἐστὶ δὲ καὶ λεπτομερὲς ἱκανῶς. τοῦτο <δὲ> τὸ φάρμακον, εἴτε ὑγρῷ σώματι προσφέροιτο δεομένῳ ξηρότητος, εἴτε ψυχρῷ δεομένῳ θερμότητος, εἴτε ἐπὶ τῶν διὰ πλήρωσιν σπωμένων, ἔνθα χρὴ κενῶσαι τὰ παρὰ φύσιν ἐν τοῖς νεύροις περιεχόμενα, μεγάλην μὲν ὠφέλειαν ἐπιδείκνυται, βλάβην δὲ οὐδεμίαν οὐδενὶ προστρίβεται μορίῳ, καὶ μάλισθ' ὅταν μὴ σφοδρῷ τινι πυρετῷ περιέχοιτο ὁ ἄνθρωπος. κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον καὶ τοῖς τρέμουσι διὰ πλῆθος ὑγρῶν παχέων καὶ γλίσχρων χυμῶν ὠφελιμώτατόν ἐστι πινόμενον. ὠφέλιμον δὲ κἀπὶ τῶν ὑπὸ λυγμοῦ ἐνοχλουμένων διὰ πλῆθος ὑγρῶν ψυχρῶν καὶ γλίσχρων ἐμπεπλασμένων τῷ στόματι τῆς γαστρός· εἰ δὲ διὰ ξηρότητα καὶ κένωσιν ἄμετρον ἢ διὰ δῆξιν δριμέων ὑγρῶν ὁ λυγμὸς ἢ σπασμὸς γίγνοντο, φεύγειν χρὴ τὴν τοῦ καστορίου χρῆσιν ὡς ἐναντιωτάτην. καὶ τῶν πυρεσσόντων δὲ τοῖς μὴ πάνυ θερμῶς πυρέττουσιν, ἀλλ' ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις χλιαρὸν ἔχουσι πυρετόν, οἷος ἐν καταφοραῖς καὶ ληθάργοις μάλιστα γίγνεται, πάνυ πολλοῖς μὲν καστόριον ἐδώκαμεν ἅμα πέπερι κοχλιάριον ἑκατέρου διὰ μελικράτου ποτίζοντες· ἐβλάβη δ' οὐδεὶς εἰς οὐδέν. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ληθαργικῶν ἢ καὶ καταφορικῶν πυρετῶν διὰ ῥοδίνου ἐλαίου δεύσαντες ἐπεθήκαμεν τῇ κεφαλῇ καὶ τῷ αὐχένι. καταμηνίων δὲ ἐπισχημένων διὰ πάχος ἐν τῷ αἵματι καὶ πλῆθος, προκενώσας ἀπὸ σφυροῦ μετρίως, εἶτα διδοὺς κοχλιάριον μετὰ γλήχωνος ἢ καλαμίνθης, ἐπειράθην ἀεὶ τοῦ φαρμάκου κινοῦντος κάθαρσιν. ἐκβάλλει δὲ καὶ χόρια κατεσχημένα καὶ τὰ δεύτερα μετὰ μελικράτου ὁμοίως πινόμενον. τοὺς δὲ ἐμπνευματουμένους τὴν γαστέρα καὶ στροφουμένους ἐπὶ παχεῖ καὶ φυσώδει πνεύματι, δι' ὀξυκράτου πινόμενον ὀνίνησι. δίδοται δὲ καὶ τοῖς ὀρθοπνοικοῖς μετ' ὀξυμέλιτος ἢ μελικράτου. καὶ ἐπ' ἀνθράκων δὲ ὑποθυμιᾶται χαίνοντος τοῦ κάμνοντος καὶ δεχομένου τὸν καπνόν.

translation: They call beavers’ testicles kastorion, a famous and much-used remedy. Here we shall state its capacity in general, by paying attention to which you can find out for yourself the detailed use. It heats and dries, and it is also sufficiently fine-particled/ of a thin consistency. This remedy should be administered either to a wet body in need of dryness, or to a cold one in need of heat, or in the case of those who are suffering from convulsions because of fullness, where one needs to evacuate unnatural things contained in the nerves. It demonstrates great benefit while not inflicting any harm on the part, and especially if the person is not in the grip of a strong fever. For the same reason it is most beneficial, when swallowed, for those who are trembling because of fullness of thick and viscous juices/humours. And it is also beneficial in the case of those who are troubled by retching because of the mass of cold and viscous fluids filling the mouth of the stomach. If the retching or the convulsions occur because of disproportionate dryness and evacuation, and because of the stinging of sharp fluids, one needs to avoid the use of kastorion as being extremely contra-indicated. And as for those among the feverish whose fever is not altogether hot, but who have - as one might say - a tepid fever, as it happens especially in kataphora and lethargos, to many of those we have given kastorion together with pepper, giving a spoonful of each to drink in melicrate. No one was harmed in any way. In cases of those suffering from lethargic and kataphoric fevers, we have mixed it with rose oil and placed it on the head and the neck. Where the menses are kept in check because of the thickness and quantity of the blood, I have always made the experienced that the remedy has moved a cleansing if I first let blood moderately from the ankle, and then gave a spoonful [of it] with pennyroyal or catmint. It also expels a retained placenta and the afterbirth when drunk in the same way with melicrate. And it helps those whose stomach is inflated and who are suffering from cramps caused by a thick and windy pneuma when it is drunk with oxycrate. It is given also to those suffering from orthopnoea, with oxymel or oxycrate. It is also burnt as incense on coals, with the patient opening the mouth wide and receiving the smoke.

greek: εἰσὶν εὔχρηστοι πρὸς ἃ καὶ οἱ τοῦ κάστορος ὄρχεις, ἀσθενέστεροι ἐκείνων μέντοι. κυνὸς δὲ ποταμίου δέρμα ὑπόδημα γενόμενον ἄκρως ποδῶν καὶ νεύρων παραμυθεῖται νόσον.

translation: Otter’s testicles. They are good to use for the same things as beaver’s testicles, but weaker than these. When the otter’s skin is made into a sandal, it perfectly soothes diseases of the feet and nerves.

translation: The puppy of a terrestrial dog. When lying down together with a person suffering from a disease of the stomach or some other [part] of the innards, it becomes a remedy for the disease by itself, taking on the affection. They say that one must bury it carefully when it has died.

greek: ἁπαλὸς ἑψηθεὶς ἐν ἐλαίῳ νεύρων ἄκος παράδοξον γίγνεται.
greek_normalized: απαλος εψηθεις εν ελαιῳ νευρων ακος παραδοξον γιγνεται.
translation: The swan nestling. A tender one boiled in oil is an admirable cure for the nerves.

greek: ξηραντικῆς ἱκανῶς ἐστι δυνάμεως· ὅθεν μιγνύμενα τοῖς ἐπιτηδείοις φαρμάκοις διαφορεῖ σκληρυνομένας φλεγμονάς· παραπλησίας δὲ ἐστι δυνάμεως καὶ τὰ τῶν πορφυρῶν καὶ τῶν ὀστρέων ὄστρακα.

translation: The burnt shells of trumpet-shells. They are of a sufficiently drying capacity. That is why, mixed with the appropriate remedies, they disperse indurated inflammations. The shells of purple snails and oysters are also of a similar capacity.

greek: τὸ σμικρόν, ὃ κατὰ τὰς ὁδοὺς πολλάκις ὁρῶμεν, ἑψόμενον ἐν λιτῷ ζωμῷ καὶ ἐσθιόμενον τοὺς κωλικοὺς ὠφελεῖ. χρὴ δὲ συνεχῶς καὶ πολλάκις ἐσθίειν αὐτὸ μετὰ τοῦ ζωμοῦ. πλειστάκις γὰρ ἐπ' αὐτῶν ἐπειράθην τῆς ἐξ αὐτοῦ ὠφελείας. ἔχει δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς τοῦτο τὸ ζῷον οἷόν τινα λόφον ἐκ τῶν πτερῶν αὐτοφυῆ.

translation: The crested lark, the winged animal. The small one, which we often see on the roads, benefits those suffering from colic, boiled in thin broth and eaten. This animal has something like a crest, naturally formed by feathers, on its head.

greek: σκληρὰν ἔχει τὴν σάρκα καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐσθιόμενος δύσπεπτος γίγνεται. ὁ δὲ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἑψομένου σκευαζόμενος ζωμὸς δι' ὕδατος καὶ ἀνήθου ἐλαίου τε καὶ γάρου ὑπέρχεται κατὰ κοιλίαν, εἰ ποθείη. εἰ δὲ ἀποχέοις τὸ πρῶτον ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ δεύτερον ἐν ᾧ ἕψεται, ἐν δὲ τῷ τρίτῳ ἑψήσα<ι>ς, μέχρι τακερὰν ἀκριβῶς γενέσθαι τὴν σάρκα καὶ δώῃς ῥευματιζομένῳ τινὶ τὴν κοιλίαν, ἐφέξει γαστέρα. ἡ δὲ ἐκ τῶν κοχλιῶν ὑγρότης μόνη καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἄνευ τῆς σαρκὸς λαμβανομένη, ἣν καλοῦσι μύξαν κοχλίου, μιγνυμένη τε λιβανωτῷ ἢ ἀλόῃ ἢ σμύρνῃ ἤ τισι τούτων ἢ πᾶσιν, ἄχρι κηρωτῆς ἔχειν πάχος, ἐχέκολλον γίγνεται τὸ φάρμακον καὶ ξηραίνει καλῶς τοὺς ὑπομύξους ὄγκους τῶν ὤτων. ἐστὶ δὲ καὶ ἀνακόλλημα ξηραντικὸν τῶν εἰς ὀφθαλμοὺς ῥευμάτων ἐπιτιθέμενον κατὰ τοῦ μετώπου· ὁπόταν μέντοι πολὺ τῆς μύξης αὐτῶν ἐθέλοις λαμβάνειν, κατακέντησον αὐτῶν τὴν σάρκα γραφίῳ· προίασι γὰρ ὑγρασίαν οὐκ ὀλίγην, καὶ μάλισθ' ὅταν μὴ πρὸ πολλῶν ἡμερῶν τεθηρευμένοι ὦσιν. ἀνακολλᾷ δὲ ἡ ὑγρότης αὕτη καὶ τὰς ἐν βλεφάροις τρίχας. ἐγὼ δὲ ποτε κατ' ἀγρὸν ἐπὶ νευροτρώτου ἅμα θλάσει γεγονότος ἐπέθηκα τὴν σάρκα τῶν κοχλιῶν, λειώσας αὐτὴν μετ' ἄχνης ἀλεύρου τῆς ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν μυλωνίων εὑρισκομένης, καὶ χωρὶς φλεγμονῆς τὸ τραῦμα ἐκολλήθη· ἦν δὲ σκληρόσαρκος ὁ ἄνθρωπος. εἰ δὲ τις εὐποροίη, κάλλιον μιγνύειν ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων σμύρναν ἢ λιβανωτὸν ἢ τὴν φρυκτὴν ῥητίνην λειοτάτην. κοπεῖσα δὲ ἡ σὰρξ ἐν ὅλμῳ πρότερον καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα λειωθεῖσα καὶ ἐπιτιθεμένη ξηραντικὴ γίγνεται πάντων τῶν περιττὴν ὑγρότητα ἐχόντων μορίων, ὡς καὶ τοῖς ὑδέροις ἁρμόττειν, καὶ σὺν τοῖς ὀστράκοις δὲ λειωθέντες οἱ κοχλίαι ἐπιτίθενται κατὰ τῆς γαστρὸς ὅλης ἐπὶ τῶν ὑδέρων, κατὰ τε τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἄρθροις ὄγκων ἐπὶ τῶν ἀρθριτικῶν· καὶ γίγνεται μὲν ἡ πρόσθεσις αὐτῶν δυσαφαίρετος, ξηραίνει δὲ ἱκανῶς. προσκεῖσθαι δὲ διὰ παντὸς αὐτοῖς προσῆκεν, ἄχρις ἂν ἀποπέσωσιν αὐτόματοι. ταὐτὸ δὲ ποιήσεις κἀπὶ τῶν δυσλύτων ἐκ πληγῆς ὄγκων ἢ ἐκ περιθλάσεως γενομένων ἐν ὠσί. ξηραίνει γὰρ ἅπαντας αὐτούς, κἂν γλίσχρον καὶ παχὺ κατὰ βάθος <ὑγρὸν> περιέχηται. ὅλοι δὲ κοχλίαι μετὰ τῶν ὀστράκων καιόμενοι, μιγνυμένης αὐτοῖς κηκίδος ὀμφακίτιδος καὶ πεπέρεως, μεγάλως ὠφελοῦσι δυσεντερίας, ἐφ' ὧν οὐδέπω ἐστὶ σηπεδονώδη τὰ ἕλκη. εἶναι δὲ χρὴ τοῦ μὲν πεπέρεως μέρος <α>, τῆς δὲ κηκίδος μέρη <β>, τέσσαρα δὲ μέρη τῆς τέφρας τῶν κοχλιῶν. ἀκριβῶς δὲ λεῖα ποιήσας ταῦτα ἅμα τε μίξας ἀπόθου, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς χρείας ἐπίπαττε ὅσον κοχλιάριον μεστὸν τοῖς ὄψοις ἢ μεθ' ὕδατος θερμοῦ ἢ δι' οἴνου δίδου πίνειν. χωρὶς δὲ τινος ἐπιμιξίας καὶ αὕτη ἡ τέφρα τῶν κεκαυμένων κοχλιῶν ξηραντικῆς ἐστι δυνάμεως, ἐχούσης τι διὰ τὴν καῦσιν καὶ θερμόν.

translation: The land snail. It has hard flesh, and because of that it is hard to digest when eaten. The broth made from it when it is boiled with water, dill, oil and garum, passes excrement the lower bowel/digestive tract when it is drunk. If you pour off the first water and the second one, in which they are boiled, and you boil them in the third until the flesh becomes tender, and give them to a person with a flux of the bowel, it will check the bowel. The moisture from the shells taken on its own, without the flesh - what they call the snail’s slime - mixed with incense and aloe and myrrh, or some of those, or all, until it has the consistency of cerate, becomes a glutinous remedy, and it beautifully dries somewhat mucous ulcers  in the ears. It is also a drying adhesive plaster for fluxes to the eyes when applied to the forehead. When you want to take much of their slime, you have to prick their flesh with a stylus. For they give off a considerable amount of moisture, and especially if they have been caught not many days ago. And this liquid also glues on the hairs in eyelashes. And once, in the country, I applied the flesh of snails on someone with a wound to a nerve that had occurred together with bruising/crushing/triturating it with the chaff of flour that is found on the walls of mills, and the wound was agglutinated without inflammation. The man was a person with hard flesh. It would be better to mix it with myrrh or frankincense, or very fine ‘roast’ resin, if one had these to hand. When the flesh is first crushed in a mortar and after that triturated and applied, it becomes drying for all parts that have a superfluous wetness, so that it is fitting even for dropsy. And the snails, triturated also with the shells, are applied over the entire stomach in cases of dropsy, and on the swellings in the joints in cases of arthritis. And when applied they become hard to remove and they dry sufficiently. It is suitable to leave them attached until they drop off on their own. You can do the same also in the case of swellings on the ears, resulting from a blow or a contusion, that are hard to reduce. For [the snails] dry all of these, even if there is a viscous and thick <wetness> contained in their depth. Burnt whole with their shells, and with oak-gall, Aleppo gall and pepper mixed in, snails greatly benefit [those suffering from] dysentery, in cases where the ulcers are not yet inclined to putrefy. It needs to be 1 part of pepper, 2 parts of oak-gall and 4 parts of ash of snails. Having carefully made those smooth, mix together and store, and in case of need sprinkle as much as a full small spoon (kochliarion) on the food, or give to drink with hot water or in wine. Even the ash of the burnt snails itself, without any addition, is of a drying capacity, containing also something hot because of the burning.

translation: Oyster shells. Unburnt and made very fine so that they become like fine powder, they are fitting for malignant ulcers, and in particular they are a most trustworthy remedy for corrosive ulcers occurring on the lips, for bringing them to cicatrisation without stinging. For they partake of a constrictive capacity, because of which they are hard and earthy, but they lose this [quality] through burning. Triturated with vinegar, or oxycrate, or oinomeli, the shells become suitable for [all things/ulcers?] inclined to putrefy - obviously when you have mixed in the liquid corresponding to the patient’s disposition. ?? CHECK Galen When burnt, the oyster shells become more fine-particled than those of trumpet-shells, because their body is also less hard than these. If their ash is washed, it becomes a useful remedy for rather wet ulcers, for filling them up and for complete cicatrisation. I, too, always use oyster shells prepared in this way for chronic concavities that are caused by fluxes and are difficult to heal, ones that are like fistulas and deep, by putting them around [the hollow] with old pig’s fat. And into the concavity itself I put one of the [substances] that build up flesh on this kind [of fistula], such as, among others, burnt talc, which they call speklarion. And the ash of oysters makes the teeth shine, like that of trumpet-shells and of purple-snails, not alone by the detergent [aspect] of its capacity, but also by the roughness of its substance. It is therefore not necessary to triturate the oyster shells strongly in these cases. They dryes moist ulcers when they are washed and made extremely fine.

greek: σηπίας ἀποπνιγείσης ὄξει, ἢν ἅμα ἐλαίῳ τὸ ὄξος δῴης πίνειν, σώσεις τὸν ἱπποκάμπου θαλαττίου φάρμακον εἰληφότα. τὸ δὲ ὄστρακον τῆς σηπίας ῥυπτικῆς καὶ ξηραντικῆς καὶ λεπτομεροῦς ἐστι δυνάμεως. διὸ καὶ καυθέντι χρώμεθα πρὸς ἀλφοὺς ἔφηλίν τε καὶ φακοὺς καὶ ψώρας. ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἀμμωνιακοῖς ἁλσὶ μιχθὲν ἀποτήκει τὰ ἐν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς πτερύγια· ἄκαυτον δὲ λεῖον ὀδόντας λαμπρύνει σμώμενον καὶ τὰς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς οὐλὰς σμήχει καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἕλκη ἀναξηραίνει καὶ τὰς ἐν τοῖς βλεφάροις μεγάλας τραχύτητας, ἃς συκώσεις καλοῦμεν, ἐκδαπανᾷ.

translation: About the cuttlefish. If you suffocate a cuttlefish in vinegar and give the vinegar to drink together with oil, you will save a person who has ingested the poison of the sea-horse. The shell of the cuttlefish is of a detergent, drying and fine-particled capacity. We therefore use it burnt for alphos, ephēlis, phakos and mange. But, mixed with rock-salt, it also removes pterygia in the eyes. Unburnt and ground, it makes the teeth shiny when used as a polish, and it wipes off scars in the eyes, and it dries up ulcers in them, and it removes the large rough patches on the eyelids that they call sukōseis.

greek: σκίγκου τὰ περὶ τοὺς νεφροὺς ὡς ἐντατικὰ τῶν αἰδοίων πίνεται καὶ ἀντιπεπονθέναι γε μάλιστα αὐτοῖς δοκεῖ θρίδακος σπέρμα μεθ' ὕδατος πινόμενον. ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ τὸ τῆς φακῆς ἀφέψημα μετὰ μέλιτος πινόμενον παύειν φασὶ τὰς ἐντάσεις τοῦ αἰδοίου.

translation: About the skink. The parts around the skink’s kidneys are swallowed as a stimulant for the genitals, and it seems that what counteracts this most is lettuce seed swallowed with water. Some also say that a decoction of beans with honey checks the swelling of the genitals.

greek: τελλίνων ταριχηρῶν καυθέντων ἡ τέφρα μετὰ κεδρίας προσαγομένη κωλύει τὰς ἐν τοῖς βλεφάροις περιττὰς τρίχας πάλιν φυῆναι.

translation: The bivalve shellfish. The ash of burnt preserved bivalve shellfish, when applied with cedar oil, prevents superfluous hairs on the eyelids from growing again.

greek: τέττιξι ξηροῖς χρῶνταὶ τινες ἐπὶ τῶν κωλικῶν διαθέσεων μετὰ πεπέρεως ἴσων τὸν ἀριθμὸν κόκκων, καὶ διδόασιν ἢ <Γ> ἢ <ε> ἢ <ζ> κατὰ τὰ διαλείμματα τῶν παροξυσμῶν. ὀπτῶντες δὲ αὐτοὺς ἄλλοι διδόασιν ἐσθίειν τοῖς πεπονθόσι τὴν κύστιν καὶ τοῖς λιθιῶσιν.

translation: The cicala. Some make use of dried cicalas in case of dispositions prone to colics, with the same number of kermes oak berries, and they give either three, or five, or seven in the intervals between attacks. Others broil them and give them to eat to those suffering from bladder problems and to those with (bladder?) stones.

greek: ὕαινα ζῶσα ἐν ἐλαίῳ ἑψομένη ὅλη, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀλωπέκων προείρηται, διαφορητικὸν ἐργάζεται τὸ ἔλαιον, χρησιμώτατον ἀρθριτικοῖς. ἡ δὲ χρῆσις γιγνέσθω ὡς ἐπὶ τῆς ἀλώπεκος προείρηται.

translation: [About the hyena.] A whole hyena boiled alive in oil - just as it has been said about foxes earlier - makes the oil dispersive, most useful for those with joint pain. It is to be used as has been said earlier about the fox.

greek: χελιδόνων τῶν πτηνῶν καιομένων ἡ τέφρα σὺν μέλιτι διαχριομένη συναγχικοὺς ἰᾶται καὶ ὅλως ὅσα κατὰ φάρυγγα καὶ γαργαρεῶνα σὺν ὄγκοις γίνεται πάθη. χρῶνται δὲ τῇ τέφρᾳ ἔνιοι καὶ πρὸς ὀξυδορκίαν ὡς ξηροκολλυρίῳ.

translation: Swallows. The ash of burnt swallows - the birds - smeared on with honey, heals those suffering from sunanchē and generally whatever affections with swellings occur in the pharynx and on the uvula. And some use the ash also as a dry collyrium for sharpening the eyesight.
